title: Is there such a thing as too much?
goal: Weigh the U-shape claim for running against pooled evidence, explain how sitting and exercise relate, and describe how healthy-volunteer bias affects cohort results.

steps.title: The U-shape claim
steps.text:
Is there such a thing as too much? Schnohr followed 1,098 healthy joggers and 3,950 healthy non-joggers in the Copenhagen City Heart Study [[c:schnohr-design]]. Against sedentary non-joggers, the death hazard ratios were:

| joggers | HR (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| light | 0.22 (0.10–0.47) |
| moderate | 0.66 (0.32–1.38) |
| strenuous | 1.97 (0.48–8.14) |

The authors called this a [U-shaped](g:u-shaped-curve) link [[c:schnohr-u]]. Look at the last row: the [confidence interval](g:confidence-interval) runs from 0.48 to 8.14, so the data fit anything from half the risk to eight times. It is not a clear sign of harm.

claims.text: Schnohr followed 1,098 healthy joggers and 3,950 healthy non-joggers from 2001.

evidence.quote: As part of the Copenhagen City Heart Study, 1,098 healthy joggers and 3,950 healthy nonjoggers have been prospectively followed up since 2001.

claims.text: Light joggers had the lowest mortality (HR 0.22) and strenuous joggers did not differ clearly from sedentary people (HR 1.97, CI 0.48–8.14); the authors describe a U-shaped association.

evidence.quote: The joggers were divided into light, moderate, and strenuous joggers. The lowest HR for mortality was found in light joggers (HR: 0.22; 95% CI: 0.10 to 0.47), followed by moderate joggers (HR: 0.66; 95% CI: 0.32 to 1.38) and strenuous joggers (HR: 1.97; 95% CI: 0.48 to 8.14).
The findings suggest a U-shaped association between all-cause mortality and dose of jogging as calibrated by pace, quantity, and frequency of jogging.

steps.title: Where the wider evidence stands
steps.text: Pedisic pooled 14 running studies from six cohorts (232,149 people). Running went with a 27% lower death rate (HR 0.73), but there was no significant dose–response trend for frequency, time, pace or total volume [[c:pedisic]]. Arem (lesson 1) found no excess risk at 10 times the guideline minimum, and Mandsager found no upper limit of fitness benefit.

claims.text: Running went with a lower death rate, and higher doses were not clearly linked to greater benefit.

evidence.quote: A meta-regression analysis showed no significant dose-response trends for weekly frequency, weekly duration, pace and the total volume of running.
Any amount of running, even just once a week, is better than no running, but higher doses of running may not necessarily be associated with greater mortality benefits.

debate.question: Does a high dose of running raise the death rate?

sides.position: Yes: risk rises again at strenuous doses (a U-shape)
No clear sign: benefit flattens and no excess risk shows up in pooled data

steps.title: Sitting versus exercise
steps.text:
Ekelund pooled 13 cohorts with sitting data (1,005,791 people). The referent group sat under 4 h a day and was in the most active quarter (over 35.5 MET-h·week⁻¹).

| group | HR |
|---|---|
| sits under 4 h, least active | 1.27 |
| sits over 8 h, least active | 1.59 |
| sits over 8 h, most active | 1.04 (0.99–1.10) |

About 60–75 min a day of moderate activity seemed to cancel the risk of long sitting [[c:sit-cancel]]. For TV time, high activity reduced but did not remove the extra risk: even the most active had higher risk at 5 h or more a day [[c:tv]]. Sitting and exercise are separate risks, and activity can offset one of them. Both are self-reported here.

claims.text: High moderate-intensity activity (about 60–75 min a day) seemed to eliminate the extra death risk of high sitting time.

evidence.quote: High levels of moderate intensity physical activity (ie, about 60-75 min per day) seem to eliminate the increased risk of death associated with high sitting time.
Daily sitting time was not associated with increased all-cause mortality in those in the most active quartile of physical activity.

claims.text: High activity reduced but did not eliminate the extra risk linked to TV-viewing time.

evidence.quote: However, this high activity level attenuates, but does not eliminate the increased risk associated with high TV-viewing time.

Watching TV for 3 h or more per day was associated with increased mortality regardless of physical activity, except in the most active quartile, where mortality was significantly increased only in people who watched TV for 5 h/day or more (HR=1·16, 1·05-1·28).

steps.title: Who joins the study?
steps.text:
[Healthy-volunteer bias](g:healthy-volunteer-bias): people who join studies are healthier than the rest. Fry compared UK Biobank, a big cohort, with the national population. Only 5.5% of those invited took part. At 70–74, mortality was 46.2% lower in men and 55.5% lower in women than in the general population [[c:fry]]. The authors call it a "healthy volunteer" bias.

They add that exposure–disease links may still hold: comparisons inside the cohort stay valid even if the cohort is healthier than average [[c:fry-ok]]. So expect absolute risks to be too low, while the shape of a dose–response curve may be sound. A runners' club study has the same issue.

claims.text: UK Biobank volunteers had much lower mortality than the general population, evidence of healthy-volunteer selection bias.

evidence.quote: At age 70-74 years, rates of all-cause mortality and total cancer incidence were 46.2% and 11.8% lower, respectively, in men and 55.5% and 18.1% lower, respectively, in women than in the general population of the same age.
UK Biobank is not representative of the sampling population; there is evidence of a "healthy volunteer" selection bias.

claims.text: Exposure–disease relationships may still be widely generalisable even if the participants are not representative.

evidence.quote: Nonetheless, valid assessment of exposure-disease relationships may be widely generalizable and does not require participants to be representative of the population at large.

steps.title: Where this leaves a keen athlete
steps.text:
| claim | status |
|---|---|
| Some activity beats none; the first minutes give most of the gain | well supported (observational, consistent) |
| Benefit levels off near 3–5× the minimum | likely |
| Excess death risk from very high doses of running or riding | not shown; data thin and mixed |
| Heart-specific effects of years of extreme endurance work | a separate question |

Death from any cause is a coarse outcome. The heart module's lessons on atrial fibrillation and coronary calcium cover the heart-specific questions, so do not read "no sign of excess deaths" as "no heart effects at all".

points: Schnohr's U-shape rests on a strenuous group with a very wide interval (0.48–8.14): suggestive, not proof of harm.
Pooled data show a lower death rate with running but no clear extra benefit at higher doses, and Arem found no excess risk at 10× the minimum.
Long sitting adds risk, and about 60–75 min of daily moderate activity cancelled it for sitting, though not fully for TV time.
Healthy-volunteer bias lowers absolute risks in cohorts, but comparisons inside the cohort may still hold.
Total mortality is a coarse outcome; heart-specific questions stay open (see the heart module).

variants.stem: Strenuous joggers had HR 1.97 (95% CI 0.48–8.14) against sedentary non-joggers. What is the fairest reading?

options.text: The interval spans 1, so harm is not shown
options.why: Right: the estimate is highly uncertain.

options.text: Strenuous jogging nearly doubles the risk of death
options.why: Takes the point estimate as fact and ignores the wide interval.

options.text: Strenuous jogging cuts risk in half
options.why: 0.48 is only the lower edge of the interval.

options.text: The result proves strenuous jogging is as safe as light jogging
options.why: The data are too uncertain to show that either.

variants.stem: Moderate joggers had HR 0.66 (95% CI 0.32–1.38) against sedentary non-joggers. What is the fairest reading?

options.text: A clear 34% lower risk of death
options.why: Takes the point estimate as fact and ignores the interval.

options.text: The interval includes 1: lower risk is not shown
options.why: Right: the interval runs from 0.32 to 1.38.

options.text: A clear 66% lower risk of death
options.why: Reads the HR as the reduction.

options.text: A clear rise in risk for moderate joggers
options.why: The estimate is below 1 and the interval is wide.

variants.stem: What shape of link between jogging dose and all-cause mortality did Schnohr's authors report?

options.text: U-shaped: light joggers did best, strenuous no better than none
options.why: Right: that is what they concluded.

options.text: A straight line: more jogging always lowers the risk
options.why: This is not the shape they reported.

options.text: Flat: the dose of jogging did not matter at all
options.why: Light joggers had a much lower rate.

options.text: An inverted U: moderate jogging was the worst dose
options.why: The opposite of what they reported.

variants.stem: What did Pedisic find about the dose of running?

options.text: Only running over 3 h a week gave any benefit
options.why: Even once a week was linked to benefit.

options.text: Any running meant lower mortality; more was not clearly better
options.why: Right: no significant trend for frequency, time, pace or volume.

options.text: Risk rose steadily with more running time
options.why: No significant dose-response trend was found.

options.text: Running had no link with mortality in these cohorts
options.why: Running went with a 27% lower rate (HR 0.73).

variants.stem: Schnohr (one city cohort, small strenuous group) says high-dose running may raise risk. Pedisic and Arem (hundreds of thousands) show no excess. How should you weigh them?

options.text: Pooled data count for more; harm is unproven but not excluded
options.why: Right: more data, but cohort limits stay.

options.text: Schnohr wins because it is more recent
options.why: Date does not decide quality.

options.text: Schnohr wins because it looked at jogging only
options.why: Narrow focus does not make it stronger than pooled data.

options.text: Pooled data prove high doses are safe
options.why: Observational data cannot prove safety.

variants.stem: A software engineer sits over 8 h a day but does more than 35.5 MET-h·week⁻¹ of cycling. A colleague sits under 4 h a day but barely moves. Which has the higher rate of death in Ekelund's data?

options.text: The colleague: HR 1.27 against 1.04 for the cyclist
options.why: Right: activity offset the sitting.

options.text: The engineer, since sitting over 8 h is always worse
options.why: In the most active group long sitting added no clear risk.

options.text: Both the same, since sitting and activity cancel out
options.why: The inactive person had a clearly higher rate (HR 1.27).

options.text: The cyclist, since high activity itself raises risk
options.why: The cyclist group had HR 1.04 (0.99–1.10), no clear rise.

variants.solution: Engineer: sits over 8 h, most active: HR 1.04 (0.99–1.10). Colleague: sits under 4 h, least active: HR 1.27 (1.22–1.31).

variants.stem: A runner works at a desk over 8 h a day and does more than 35.5 MET-h·week⁻¹. Another person sits over 8 h and is in the least active quarter. Which has the higher death rate?

options.text: The runner, since long sitting always adds risk
options.why: In the most active group long sitting added no clear risk.

options.text: The inactive person: HR 1.59 against 1.04
options.why: Right: the runner's activity offsets the sitting.

options.text: Both the same, since sitting decides risk
options.why: The least active, long-sitting group had HR 1.59.

options.text: The runner, since high activity raises risk
options.why: The runner's HR was 1.04, no clear rise.

variants.stem: In Ekelund's data, high activity cancelled the risk of long sitting but not of 5 h or more of TV. What does that suggest?

options.text: Activity offsets sitting risk, but TV time may carry extra risk
options.why: Right: activity attenuated but did not eliminate TV risk.

options.text: TV is harmless if you exercise
options.why: High activity attenuated but did not eliminate the TV risk.

options.text: Sitting at work is worse than TV
options.why: The data say nothing of the sort.

options.text: The result is chance because TV data were self-reported only
options.why: Self-report is a limit, but it does not explain the pattern.

options.text: People who drop out of a study are always sicker
options.why: This is attrition, a different problem.

options.text: People who join a study are healthier than the general population
options.why: Right: so absolute risks look too low.

options.text: Researchers pick only the healthiest people to enrol
options.why: The bias arises from who volunteers, not researcher choice.

options.text: People get healthier because a study watches them
options.why: That would be an effect of being studied, not a bias in who joins.

variants.stem: A cycling-club cohort has a death rate half that of the national population. What is the right caution?

options.text: Absolute risk is too low; comparisons inside the club may still hold
options.why: Right: this is Fry's point.

options.text: The cohort is useless for any question
options.why: Fry says internal comparisons may still hold.

options.text: The club proves cycling halves death risk
options.why: Volunteers are healthier to begin with.

options.text: The result is wrong because clubs are small
options.why: Size is not the issue; who joins is.

variants.stem: A running-club cohort has a death rate 40% below the national rate. What is the right caution?

options.text: The cohort is useless for any question
options.why: Fry says internal comparisons may still hold.

options.text: The club proves running cuts death risk by 40%
options.why: Volunteers are healthier to begin with.

options.text: Absolute risk is too low; comparisons inside the club may still hold
options.why: Right: this is Fry's point.

options.text: The result is wrong because clubs are small
options.why: Size is not the issue; who joins is.

variants.stem: A cohort finds no excess deaths at 10 times the guideline minimum. What does this show about extreme endurance and the heart?

options.text: Little: death from any cause is coarse and may hide heart-specific effects
options.why: Right: the heart questions need their own evidence.

options.text: It proves there are no heart effects at all
options.why: Total mortality cannot show this.

options.text: It proves extreme doses are healthier than moderate
options.why: The curve flattened; it did not show extreme was best.

options.text: It shows the heart is unaffected below 10 times
options.why: The study did not look at heart structure or rhythm.
